question: Can translation, rotation, and independent input/output scale invariance plus a regularity index define a rigorous parameter-light Bayesian regression process, and do its posterior, uncertainty, extrapolation, speed, and empirical-parity claims follow from the stated mathematics and experiments?

key_findings.claim: The paper derives a compact scale-free spline formalism, but the supposedly minimal prior is both improper and selected by an additional unproved simplicity judgment.
key_findings.evidence: Finite-dimensional output-scale invariance forces radial density proportional to 1/r^ν, whose radial integral is proportional to the integral of dr/r and diverges at both zero and infinity. The functional equation leaves angular behavior free; the paper cannot use maximum entropy for an improper distribution and calls ellipsoidal symmetry the 'obvious' simplest choice. Input-scale invariance then motivates a power-law spectrum indexed by η, together with translation, rotation, Euclidean geometry, stationarity, isotropy, and regularity assumptions. These are an interpretable collection of inductive biases, not an assumption-free prior.

anchors.section: Sections 2.3-2.6 spectrum, regularity, and function space

key_findings.claim: For noiseless interpolation away from the nullspace, the construction recovers a useful polyharmonic-spline mean and a formal Student-t conditional with data-dependent scale.
key_findings.evidence: The Green functions are radial powers ||x−ξ||^(2η). Linear coefficient constraints cancel divergent low-frequency terms, leaving a data-spanned subspace of dimension N−N0, where N0 counts polynomial nullspace monomials. Solving the block Green-function/polynomial system yields the minimum-seminorm polyharmonic interpolant. Formally conditioning the hyperbolic finite-dimensional density on a nonzero data vector produces a multivariate Student-t law with ν=N−N0 and a pointwise scale proportional to the interpolant seminorm divided by a test-function seminorm.

anchors.section: Sections 3.1-3.4 Green functions, constraints, and posterior process

key_findings.claim: The Gaussian-noise regression posterior is not normalizable, so its reported mean, covariance, credible intervals, and samples are a local pole-avoiding heuristic rather than moments of the stated Bayesian posterior.
key_findings.evidence: In the Nh-dimensional data-spanned subspace, the prior has density ||h||^(−Nh); the volume element therefore leaves a radial integral proportional to dr/r near h=0. A Gaussian likelihood that is finite and positive at the origin cannot remove this logarithmic divergence. The manuscript explicitly says the nullspace pole retains infinite probability mass and that, strictly speaking, SIP regression reduces to polynomial regression; it then initializes NUTS on a separated likelihood bump and says sampling never encounters the pole. An unnormalized posterior has no posterior expectation or covariance, and avoiding its singular region computationally does not define the claimed distribution.

anchors.section: Section 5 NUTS initialization and sampling protocol

key_findings.claim: The existence of an infinite-dimensional improper stochastic process is asserted beyond what the cited consistency calculation establishes.
key_findings.evidence: The paper invokes Daniell-Kolmogorov and immediately acknowledges that it knows of no theory of improper processes. Appendix 8.1 shows a scale-homogeneity relation for hyperplane integrals of an infinite measure, but does not construct consistent normalized probability measures or justify conditioning, countable additivity, and almost-sure statements in the infinite-dimensional limit. The finite conditional Student-t algebra at nonzero observations can still be useful, but it does not validate the claimed prior process.

key_findings.claim: The regularity theorem is not established by the appendix argument and is especially problematic for η greater than one.
key_findings.evidence: Appendix 8.2 represents a general fractional Laplacian using only the first difference f(x)−f(ξ), then rewrites η regularity as |f(x)−f(ξ)|≤C||x−ξ||^η. For η>1 that first-difference Hölder condition does not express floor(η) differentiability plus Hölder continuity of the highest derivative and, on connected domains, is generally too strong. The inequalities supply at most a sufficient integrability direction but are promoted to an equivalence; they also assume finite η-norm almost surely under the undefined improper process. Thus the advertised sample differentiability for all positive noninteger η needs a different, rigorous proof with the appropriate higher-order differences or derivative spaces.

anchors.section: Appendix 8.2 spectral argument and claimed equivalence

key_findings.claim: A norm identity required by the inference algorithm is proved only for positive half-integer η, while two central evaluated variants use an explicitly conjectured extension.
key_findings.evidence: Equations 36-37 convert polyharmonic coefficients into the η-seminorm used for orthonormalization and uncertainty. The main text says the formula is proved for positive half-integers and supported only by numerical evidence otherwise. Appendix 8.5 indeed ends with a half-integer sine-integral derivation and conjectures replacement of the factorial by a Gamma function for all positive nonintegers. Table 1 nevertheless evaluates η=1.01 and η=2.01, and η=1.01 is the best SIP choice on marathon and Boston, so the unproved extension affects headline results rather than a peripheral option.

key_findings.claim: The reported uncertainty is an unvalidated approximation to a formal mixture, and even the displayed standard-deviation formula requires more data than the paper's stated minimum.
key_findings.evidence: The exact claimed regression posterior is a mixture of t-processes over sampled h*. For use, the paper replaces it by one t-process centered at the sampled mean and adds an interpolation variance to a transformed sample covariance; it provides no derivation that this moment combination equals the mixture, no numerical approximation error, and no coverage, calibration, log-score, or Bayesian-optimization evaluation. The pointwise t standard deviation divides by sqrt(ν−2), requiring ν=N−N0>2, whereas the text states only N≥N0+1 for a nondegenerate conditional. Equation 57 also leaves the test-vector mapping insufficiently specified for independent reproduction.

anchors.section: Equations 38-41 pointwise t scale and standard deviation
Section 4.6 mixture approximation and variance decomposition

key_findings.claim: The benchmark supports only rough RMSE parity on seven small tabular datasets and exposes substantial sensitivity to η.
key_findings.evidence: Table 1 reports one 5-fold cross-validation RMSE per method on datasets ranging from 27 to 1,599 points, comparing five GP kernels with five SIP η values. No fold dispersion, repeated split, seed uncertainty, statistical test, predictive likelihood, or nested selection protocol is given. Best entries in the two families are often close, but SIP η=5/2 is missing for diabetes and degrades sharply on marathon, Boston, concrete, and red wine, reaching RMSE 30.49 on concrete versus about 5.6 for useful variants. The evidence therefore does not support a general equal-performance or low-sensitivity claim.

key_findings.claim: Better extrapolation is illustrated but not measured, and the same examples reveal uncontrolled outlier and nonstationarity behavior.
key_findings.evidence: Figure 4 uses one synthetic step dataset that the authors say is unsuitable for both vanilla GP and SIP. It shows SIP uncertainty expanding outside the observed range while a stationary GP returns to a fitted mean and constant variance, but supplies no true out-of-range function, extrapolation error, coverage, or proper score. The marathon full-data plot shows the 1904 outlier causing a noticeable kink in SIP but not GP. These visuals motivate an OOD study; they do not establish superior extrapolation or robustness.

anchors.section: Figure 5 marathon fit and outlier observation

key_findings.claim: The speed advantage is prospective and contradicted by the implemented procedure's own cost profile.
key_findings.evidence: Constructing and inverting dense systems retains O(N^3) complexity. Each reported SIP fit uses two PyMC3 NUTS chains of 1,000 draws with half discarded, while GP hyperparameters are optimized with GPy defaults. The paper supplies no wall-clock or memory comparison and explicitly calls its baseline sampler quite slow and unable to realize the claimed potential. Eliminating GP kernel optimization is therefore not evidence that the present SIP implementation is faster.

anchors.section: Practical advantages and explicit slow-sampler caveat

key_findings.claim: The likelihood specification contains a sign error and omits a normalization term that becomes consequential when the noise scale is sampled.
key_findings.evidence: Equation 49 visually prints the Gaussian quadratic with a positive exponent, which would grow away from its mean and be nonintegrable; Equation 51 uses the expected negative sign, strongly suggesting a typographical error. Equation 49 is also written only up to proportionality without the determinant or σ-dependent Gaussian normalization. That omission is harmless for fixed covariance but not when Section 4.5 samples σ under a 1/σ prior unless the implementation restores the σ^(−N) factor. No implementation is released to resolve which density was actually sampled.

anchors.section: Equations 49-52 likelihood, posterior, and unknown noise

key_findings.claim: The durable novelty is a symmetry-motivated route to a fractional polyharmonic t-process heuristic, not the discovery of spline-GP equivalence, t-process regression, or a validated parameter-free Bayesian method.
key_findings.evidence: The paper itself cites the classical correspondence among stochastic-process Bayes estimates, differential penalties, kriging, and splines. Before its submission, proper Student-t processes already offered analytic predictive distributions and data-dependent covariance, and flat-limit GP theory showed convergence of both predictive means and variances to polynomial or polyharmonic spline regression. Later improper-GP work gives analytically conditionable non-mean-reverting posteriors, while a 2025 random-function derivation reaches a generalized polyharmonic spline from related symmetry postulates. The target's distinctive combination is output-scale hyperbolicity, fractional η, and a proposed noisy-regression sampler, but the latter is not a normalized posterior.

anchors.section: Related spline, differential-operator, and GP theory

method.core_idea: Replace a chosen covariance amplitude and length scale with independent input/output scale invariance, impose Euclidean translation and rotation invariance plus a regularity index η, derive a power-law seminorm and polyharmonic Green functions, and perform interpolation or noisy regression using a hyperbolic improper prior over the data-spanned function coefficients.
method.mechanism: A ν-dimensional scale-invariant density proportional to the inverse ν-th power of an ellipsoidal radius is extended formally to function values. A stationary power spectrum proportional to ||k||^(−η−D/2) defines an η-seminorm with a polynomial nullspace. Constrained radial Green-function combinations yield a polyharmonic spline interpolant and formal Student-t conditionals. For noisy data, the method constructs an η-orthonormal basis, combines a hyperbolic prior on non-null coefficients and a uniform polynomial prior with a Gaussian likelihood, samples coefficients and an optional Jeffreys-prior noise scale using NUTS, and approximates the resulting claimed mixture of t-processes by a single t-process with two additive variance components.
assumptions: Input and output spaces have meaningful Euclidean translation, rotation, and scale symmetries.
Input and output scale changes should be independently invariant rather than jointly self-similar.
Ellipsoidal symmetry is the simplest angular completion of radial scale invariance.
An improper finite-dimensional density can be extended and conditioned as an infinite-dimensional stochastic process.
Kolmogorov-style marginal consistency remains sufficient for unnormalized infinite measures.
A stationary isotropic power-law spectrum is the correct consequence of no distinguished input scale.
One noninteger regularity parameter η adequately represents the target function.
Polynomial components below degree η should receive an improper uniform prior.
The generalized polyharmonic Green function ||x−ξ||^(2η) is valid for the chosen fractional η.
The half-integer spline-norm identity extends to all positive noninteger η by replacing a factorial with a Gamma function.
Gaussian observation noise is appropriate after min-max feature scaling and optional jitter.
A 1/σ noise-scale prior yields usable inference despite its interpolation pole.
NUTS initialized on the likelihood bump can ignore the nullspace and interpolation poles without changing the inferential target.
The mean and covariance of samples from that local branch can be called posterior moments.
A single t-process with added variance components sufficiently approximates the claimed mixture.
Min-max scaling all features to equal range is an acceptable substitute for automatic relevance determination.
Five candidate η values and standard GP kernels provide a fair model-family comparison.
Small legacy tabular datasets are informative about general regression, extrapolation, and computational behavior.

techniques.role: Uses a hyperbolic radial density so output rescaling changes density only by the volume Jacobian.
Encodes input-scale invariance and regularity through an isotropic power-law amplitude spectrum.
Defines a homogeneous Fourier seminorm whose nullspace contains low-degree polynomials.
Builds radial Green functions proportional to ||x−ξ||^(2η).
Constrains Green-function coefficients so divergent low-frequency Taylor terms cancel.
Solves a block radial-basis and polynomial system for the minimum-seminorm interpolant.
Constructs a minimum-seminorm function vanishing on training points to map formal t coordinates to pointwise uncertainty.
Sequentially constructs an η-orthonormal basis of the data-spanned subspace.
Samples coefficients and optional observation noise on a likelihood bump separated from acknowledged singular poles.
Represents the claimed full predictive law as a coefficient-weighted mixture of t-processes.
Approximates mixture uncertainty by adding interpolation and transformed spline variances.
Min-max scales features and jitters discrete values to improve numerical conditioning without ARD.
Compares five fixed η choices against five optimized stationary GP kernel families.

evaluations.metric: Scale transformation law, marginal homogeneity, and analytic conditional form
evaluations.result: The density has the intended radial scale law, hyperplane marginals retain that homogeneity, and conditioning a nonzero finite vector gives a Student-t-shaped conditional.
evaluations.baseline: The source does not construct normalized finite marginals or a probability process; it explicitly notes the absence of improper-process theory.

evaluations.metric: Block-system solution and formal pointwise Student-t posterior
evaluations.result: The predictive center is a constrained polyharmonic spline with ν=N−N0 and data-dependent scale.
evaluations.baseline: This connects to established spline, kriging, intrinsic-random-function, and Student-t-process theory; only the target's specific improper scale construction is new.

evaluations.metric: NUTS samples from two 1,000-draw chains, discarding 500 per chain
evaluations.result: Samples initialized at the likelihood mean produce a finite empirical mean and covariance on the separated local bump.
evaluations.baseline: The stated posterior has infinite mass at h=0 and, with unknown noise, at interpolation; local pole avoidance does not yield draws from a normalized posterior.

evaluations.result: The best SIP and best GP entries are often numerically close across marathon, diabetes, Boston, two energy targets, concrete, and red wine.
evaluations.baseline: There are no repeated splits, uncertainty intervals, tests, nested selection, log scores, or calibration metrics, and the datasets contain only 27-1,599 observations.

evaluations.result: Several η values are competitive, but η=5/2 is missing on diabetes and fails badly on multiple datasets, including concrete RMSE 30.49.
evaluations.baseline: The claim that η only indirectly and weakly affects regularization is not supported by this failure pattern.

evaluations.metric: Visual posterior mean and spline, function, and data uncertainty bands
evaluations.result: SIP uncertainty grows outside observations and its mean does not revert to a fitted global mean, while the stationary GP exhibits mean reversion.
evaluations.baseline: No out-of-range targets, errors, coverage, or proper scores are supplied, and the authors call both methods unsuitable for the step data.

evaluations.metric: Visual comparison of best GP and SIP mean and uncertainty
evaluations.result: Both produce plausible smooth trends, but the 1904 outlier creates a visible kink in SIP and little visible effect in GP.
evaluations.baseline: This is a full-data visualization rather than a robustness or extrapolation test.

evaluations.metric: Visual fit on one sandbox dataset
evaluations.result: The finite local mode has much smaller η-norm and overregularizes relative to the empirical sampled mean.
evaluations.baseline: The density is globally unbounded at the nullspace pole, so the plotted 'maximum posterior' is necessarily a local finite branch.

evaluations.metric: Qualitative paths generated by sequential pointwise Student-t conditioning
evaluations.result: η=3/2 paths look similar to Matérn-3/2 GP paths.
evaluations.baseline: No distributional calibration or comparison of joint samples is reported, and the generation procedure is described as expensive.

evaluations.metric: Asymptotic complexity and qualitative optimization discussion
evaluations.result: Dense SIP algebra is O(N^3), like exact GP regression, and avoids explicit GP kernel-parameter optimization.
evaluations.baseline: No timing or memory benchmark is given; the implemented NUTS procedure is explicitly slow and is compared with default GP optimization rather than matched inference budgets.

limitations: The finite-dimensional prior is improper at both zero and infinity.
The noisy-regression posterior remains improper at the nullspace pole even after applying the likelihood.
The optional 1/σ noise prior creates another infinite-mass pole at exact interpolation.
NUTS intentionally stays on a separated likelihood bump and therefore does not sample the stated global posterior.
The existence of an improper infinite-dimensional stochastic process is not established by a probability-measure extension theorem.
Almost-sure sample-path claims are not well-defined without a proper process measure.
Ellipsoidal symmetry is justified as 'obvious' rather than derived from an entropy or decision principle.
The regularity proof uses a first-difference Hölder expression that does not represent higher-order differentiability for η>1.
The appendix moves from sufficient bounds to an asserted equivalence without proving both directions.
The spline inner-product constant is proved only for half-integer η and conjectured for other evaluated values.
Positive integer η is excluded, and the paper's challenge to the conventional logarithmic polyharmonic solution is deferred rather than resolved.
The mixture-of-t-process posterior is replaced by a single-process variance approximation without accuracy analysis.
Displayed t standard deviations require N−N0>2, stronger than the stated nondegeneracy minimum.
Equation 49 has the wrong sign in the likelihood exponent and does not display the noise-scale normalization needed for Section 4.5.
Only seven small legacy regression datasets are evaluated.
Cross-validation splits, random seeds, fold-level scores, and uncertainty across runs are not reported.
Model-family selection is not nested, despite comparing five η values and five GP kernels.
No predictive likelihood, calibration, coverage, sharpness, or Bayesian-optimization metric tests uncertainty quality.
The extrapolation claim rests on one qualitative step-function plot without out-of-domain targets.
The method is stationary and isotropic and has no automatic relevance determination.
All features are min-max scaled to equal range and discrete features receive arbitrary 0.1% jitter.
Dense algebra remains cubic and the sampling implementation is acknowledged to be slow.
No source code, environment specification, dataset split artifact, or author-hosted implementation is cited in the paper.
failure_modes: A sampler can appear stable by never reaching an infinite-density pole, while its finite empirical moments have no global posterior meaning.
Calling a local likelihood bump the posterior can conceal that the true improper model collapses to its polynomial nullspace.
With an improper noise-scale prior, interpolation can absorb infinite mass and make finite-noise samples initialization-dependent.
Using Equation 49 literally would make the likelihood increase with squared error.
Dropping the Gaussian σ-dependent normalization can change the sampled noise posterior.
A conjectured fractional-η norm constant can alter basis scaling, likelihood geometry, and credible intervals.
For too few points, a formal Student-t conditional may exist while its variance is infinite or undefined.
Selecting the lowest RMSE across η on the same folds can make parameter-light inference look stronger than held-out model selection would.
A high η can be numerically unstable or grossly overfit or underfit, as the η=5/2 results demonstrate.
Feature range scaling can hide anisotropy and make results depend on arbitrary preprocessing bounds.
Jittering discrete covariates changes the geometry that the invariance derivation assumes.
Growing uncertainty outside the data can look qualitatively desirable while being badly calibrated or paired with a biased mean.
A polyharmonic spline can react strongly to isolated observations, producing kinks or poor transfer.
Dense O(N^3) systems and NUTS can erase any saving from avoiding kernel optimization.
Stationarity and isotropy can fail on heterogeneous, manifold, categorical, or locally varying tasks.
An unnormalized finite-dimensional family can satisfy formal scaling and marginal algebra without defining a coherent stochastic process.
reusable_insights: When evolving RL environments, treat symmetry constraints as explicit environment-design priors rather than as absence of assumptions.
Prove that every proposed task distribution, reward prior, and evaluator distribution is normalizable before interpreting samples or expectations.
Audit singular reward or fitness regions analytically; an optimizer that never visits a pole may still be optimizing only an initialization-dependent local branch.
Use invariances to reduce environment-search dimension only after checking that they preserve the intended task semantics.
A formal oracle can eliminate humans for mechanical validity checks, but human review remains valuable for whether the encoded symmetry and reward represent a useful and safe skill.
Validate an environment's learning signal with held-out procedural seeds, agent families, budgets, and capacities rather than one small solver.
Measure reward-signal calibration, ranking stability, exploit rate, and OOD transfer in addition to final return.
Do not claim scaling from a small model solely because the same task can be instantiated at larger size; test rank correlation and mechanism persistence across multiple model scales.
If full-scale training is expensive, use multi-fidelity curves and early learning progress, then prospectively validate which proxy rankings survive at larger budgets.
Keep environment generation, validity checks, reward-hacking tests, solver evaluation, and human semantic review as separate modules with explicit interfaces.
Use nested held-out tasks when selecting an environment regularity, difficulty, or generator parameter so the selection budget is not counted as validation.
Record failed environment parameters and missing runs; catastrophic settings are evidence about robustness, not values to omit from an average.
Evaluate uncertainty or learning-signal estimates with coverage, proper scores, and decision quality rather than attractive widening bands alone.
Require an executable artifact with pinned dependencies, seeds, splits, and pole or boundary diagnostics before using a proposed Bayesian evaluator inside evolutionary search.
open_questions: Can a proper heavy-tailed or truncated radial prior preserve approximate output-scale invariance while yielding a normalizable regression posterior?
Can σ-finite measure theory rigorously define the claimed finite and infinite-dimensional conditionals, and which observables remain identifiable?
How do predictions change as an explicit cutoff around the nullspace pole is varied toward zero?
Does a regularized proper model converge to the sampled likelihood-bump branch or to polynomial regression in any principled limit?
Can the regularity result be reproved with Besov or Sobolev spaces, higher-order differences, and valid fractional-Laplacian domains?
Is the Gamma-function extension of the polyharmonic inner-product constant true for all positive noninteger η used by the algorithm?
What is the correct scale-invariant treatment at positive integer η and how does it relate to logarithmic polyharmonic splines and intrinsic random functions?
Can the full mixture of t-processes be computed or approximated with quantified error and calibrated predictive intervals?
What minimum sample-size conditions guarantee finite predictive means, variances, and higher moments?
Does SIP remain competitive under nested hyperparameter selection, repeated splits, larger modern datasets, and predictive log-score evaluation?
Does the expanding OOD variance improve actual extrapolation error, interval coverage, Bayesian optimization regret, or environment-search decisions?
Can anisotropic, nonstationary, categorical, or manifold variants retain a coherent subset of the proposed invariances?
Can structured linear algebra or a proper conjugate construction deliver a measured speed advantage over optimized and approximate GPs?
Which diagnostics reliably distinguish samples from a normalized posterior from samples confined to a metastable likelihood branch?
For synthetic RL environments, when do invariance-derived generators preserve solver rankings across scale, and when do they create exploitable degeneracies?

competitive_landscape.title: Student-t Processes as Alternatives to Gaussian Processes
competitive_landscape.difference: Shah, Wilson, and Ghahramani derive proper Student-t processes through an inverse-Wishart-process hierarchy, with closed-form marginal likelihood and prediction, data-dependent predictive covariance, analytic model selection, and no extra asymptotic cost over a GP. SIP removes explicit amplitude and length-scale choices through an improper hyperbolic construction, but loses posterior propriety and analytic noisy inference.

competitive_landscape.title: State Space Methods for Efficient Inference in Student-t Process Regression
competitive_landscape.difference: Solin and Särkkä retain a proper canonical Student-t process and derive closed-form temporal inference with linear-time state-space filtering and smoothing. SIP applies to general Euclidean inputs and derives a polyharmonic mean, but keeps cubic dense algebra and slow MCMC, so its speed claim does not supersede this structured alternative.

competitive_landscape.title: Adaptive empirical Bayesian smoothing splines
competitive_landscape.difference: Serra and Krivobokova select both smoothing penalty and order by empirical Bayes and study adaptive credible sets with frequentist coverage. SIP aims to avoid a smoothing-scale parameter and permits fractional polyharmonic order, but provides neither a proper posterior nor coverage theory and still exposes η as a consequential choice.

competitive_landscape.title: Adaptive Bayesian credible sets in regression with a Gaussian process prior
competitive_landscape.difference: Sniekers and van der Vaart analyze empirical and hierarchical Bayes scale adaptation, posterior contraction, and credible-set coverage under explicit self-similarity conditions. SIP offers a symmetry-motivated scale-free heuristic but does not test coverage or establish contraction, so widening its bands is not comparable evidence of calibrated uncertainty.

competitive_landscape.title: Robust Gaussian Stochastic Process Emulation
competitive_landscape.difference: Gu, Wang, and Berger study objective priors, anisotropic kernels, robust parameterizations, a nugget, and posterior propriety for Gaussian stochastic-process emulation. SIP more aggressively removes range and variance parameters and assumes isotropy, but its improper posterior shows why objective-prior simplicity must be paired with explicit propriety analysis.

competitive_landscape.title: Propriety of the reference posterior distribution in Gaussian Process modeling
competitive_landscape.difference: Muré proves that a reference prior yields proper GP posteriors for smooth squared-exponential, Matérn, and rational-quadratic kernels and derives tail behavior. SIP argues from invariance but knowingly retains infinite mass; this work makes posterior propriety, not sampler pole avoidance, the relevant objective-Bayes standard.

competitive_landscape.title: Can we trust Bayesian uncertainty quantification from Gaussian process priors with squared exponential covariance kernel?
competitive_landscape.difference: Hadji and Szabó show that GP scale selection can yield overconfident credible sets and analyze modifications that recover coverage under restrictions. SIP criticizes GP extrapolation visually, but supplies no analogous coverage audit and uses moments from an improper local branch, making this calibration framework a necessary competing standard.

competitive_landscape.title: Gaussian Process Regression in the Flat Limit
competitive_landscape.difference: Barthelmé, Amblard, Tremblay, and Usevich show that flat-limit GP regression converges to polynomial or polyharmonic-spline regression in both predictive mean and variance, and connect the limit to leave-one-out model choice. This predates SIP's submission and narrows its novelty: SIP offers a different symmetry and heavy-tail derivation, not the first Bayesian polyharmonic predictive process.

competitive_landscape.title: Bayesian online change point detection with Hilbert space approximate Student-t process
competitive_landscape.difference: Sellier and Dellaportas combine an analytically tractable Student-t process with a Hilbert-space reduced-rank Laplacian representation and demonstrate prediction and training-time gains. Its change-point scope differs, but it supplies released, measured scalable heavy-tailed inference where SIP only predicts a future speed advantage.

competitive_landscape.title: Stationarity without mean reversion in improper Gaussian processes
competitive_landscape.relationship: closest rigorous improper-process and extrapolation successor
competitive_landscape.difference: Ambrogioni uses improper infinite-variance GP limits and non-positive kernels to obtain stationary, non-mean-reverting models with analytic corrected posterior formulas and synthetic and real experiments. SIP reaches non-mean-reverting polyharmonic behavior through output-scale hyperbolicity, but its noisy posterior remains unnormalized and sampled rather than analytically conditioned.

competitive_landscape.title: Robust and Conjugate Gaussian Process Regression
competitive_landscape.difference: Altamirano, Briol, and Knoblauch use generalized Bayes to robustify GP regression while preserving exact conjugate updates at virtually no additional cost, with applications including Bayesian optimization. It retains a kernel but directly delivers proper computational and robustness evidence absent from SIP's slow pole-avoiding sampler and outlier-sensitive marathon example.

competitive_landscape.title: Online Student-t Processes with an Overall-local Scale Structure for Modelling Non-stationary Data
competitive_landscape.difference: Sha and Zhang use an adaptive mixture of Student-t processes with overall-local covariance and noise scales plus sequential Monte Carlo for online nonstationary heavy-tailed data. The extra structure is less minimalist, but it directly targets nonstationarity and local scale variation that SIP lists as unresolved and demonstrates synthetic and real-data results.

competitive_landscape.title: Solving a Machine Learning Regression Problem Based on the Theory of Random Functions
competitive_landscape.difference: Bakhvalov independently derives a generalized polyharmonic spline from translation, rotation, scaling, Gaussianity, and indifference postulates in random-function theory, explicitly identifying SIP as a related non-Gaussian route. As a 2025 preprint it requires scrutiny, but its use of a probability-measure framework directly competes with SIP's unsupported improper-process extension.

competitive_landscape.title: Polyharmonic Spline Packages: Composition, Efficient Procedures for Computation and Differentiation
competitive_landscape.difference: Bakhvalov explicitly starts from the cubic cost and high-dimensional limitations of symmetry-derived polyharmonic regression and proposes differentiable packages and cascades for scalable computation. The preprint does not validate SIP's uncertainty model, but it is a direct current alternative to the target's unrealized promise of faster practical polyharmonic learning.

novelty_assessment.author_claim: The paper claims that independent input/output scale invariance, translation and rotation invariance, and a regularity degree are enough to derive a novel non-Gaussian stochastic process and Bayesian regression method with a polyharmonic-spline mean, mixture-of-t-process posterior, equal GP performance, no regularization parameter, potential speed, and better extrapolation.
novelty_assessment.evidence: The manuscript supplies finite-dimensional scale algebra, a power-law Fourier seminorm, polynomial-nullspace and Green-function constructions, formal Student-t interpolation conditionals, a NUTS-based noisy-regression procedure, seven small 5-fold RMSE benchmarks, one synthetic extrapolation visualization, and appendix derivations through Equation 141.
novelty_assessment.reviewer_inference: The distinctive contribution is an unusually direct symmetry-motivated path from an output-scale hyperbolic density and fractional input spectrum to polyharmonic interpolation and data-dependent formal t uncertainty. Classical work already links stochastic processes, splines, kriging, and differential penalties; proper Student-t processes predate the paper, and flat-limit GP theory already reaches polyharmonic predictive means and variances. More importantly, the noisy posterior retains infinite mass, so the sampled likelihood bump is not Bayesian inference under the stated model; process existence, higher-order regularity, a fractional norm constant, interval calibration, extrapolation, and speed are also unproved or untested. Current successors offer analytically conditioned improper GPs, robust conjugate GPs, adaptive Student-t processes, and another symmetry-to-polyharmonic derivation. The result is therefore a provocative mathematical heuristic and useful research direction, not a validated parameter-free Bayesian replacement for GP regression.

reviewer_notes: Read all 17 pages of the exact hash-pinned source, including the main paper, Table 1, all seven figures, all 141 numbered equations, references, additional results, and every supplementary proof. An all-page contact-sheet audit found no blank, duplicated, clipped, or unreadable page; original-resolution inspection covered the posterior geometry and likelihood equations on page 6, uncertainty and nonstationary plots on page 7, the benchmark table on page 8, all supplementary figures on pages 10-11, the regularity argument on pages 12-13, and the coefficient and inner-product derivations on pages 14-17. Equation 49's positive exponent and Equation 105's missing x−xn argument were verified visually rather than inferred from extraction. Source-lineage caveat: the cache is exactly the current arXiv:2208.10461v3 PDF, revised 2022-10-29; downloading the explicit v3 route on 2026-08-23 reproduced SHA-256 5ed1362f1a556033d40d36d97cb34ca3d4bf68eac198974e50e490f5b36e1cb8 byte for byte. This record is bound only to those cached v3 bytes. Fourteen primary arXiv and PMLR competitor records were checked through 2026-08-23, spanning proper Student-t processes, objective-prior propriety, adaptive spline and GP coverage, flat-limit polyharmonic prediction, non-mean-reverting improper GPs, robust conjugate inference, adaptive nonstationary t-processes, and direct 2025 symmetry-derived polyharmonic successors. The source cites PyMC3 and GPy but no implementation; an exact-title and identifier search did not locate an author-hosted SIP code release, so no artifact was executable in this audit. No projection or generated synopsis was used.
